questions.questionText: For the projection matrix P that projects vectors in ℝ³ onto the xy‑plane, which statement about its eigenvalues and eigenvectors is correct?
options: All vectors in the xy‑plane are eigenvectors with eigenvalue 0.
The normal vector (0,0,1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1.
Vectors in the xy‑plane are eigenvectors with eigenvalue 1, and the normal vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.
No non‑zero eigenvectors exist for P.
questions.correctAnswer: Vectors in the xy‑plane are eigenvectors with eigenvalue 1, and the normal vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.
questions.explanation: Projecting a vector already in the xy‑plane leaves it unchanged, so λ=1 for those vectors; projecting the z‑axis vector gives the zero vector, so λ=0 for (0,0,1).
questions.subtopic: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of projection matrices

questions.questionText: Given the matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix}4&-5\\2&-3\end{pmatrix}\), which statement about the relationship between its eigenvalues and its trace is correct?
options: The sum of the eigenvalues equals 7.
The sum of the eigenvalues equals 1.
The sum of the eigenvalues equals -1.
The sum of the eigenvalues equals 0.
questions.correctAnswer: The sum of the eigenvalues equals 1.
questions.explanation: The trace of a matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries: 4+(-3)=1. For any square matrix, the sum of its eigenvalues (counting multiplicities) equals the trace, so the eigenvalues of A sum to 1.

questions.questionText: If a 2×2 matrix has eigenvalues λ₁ = 2 and λ₂ = −1, what is the determinant of the matrix?
questions.explanation: For any square matrix, the product of its eigenvalues equals its determinant. Here 2 × (−1) = −2.

questions.questionText: Consider the 2×2 matrix Q that represents a counter‑clockwise rotation by 90° in the plane. Which statement about its eigenvalues and eigenvectors over the real numbers is correct?
options: Q has two distinct real eigenvalues, 1 and -1, with corresponding eigenvectors.
Q has a single real eigenvalue 0, and all vectors are eigenvectors.
Q has no real eigenvalues, and therefore no non‑zero real eigenvectors.
Q has real eigenvalues 0 and 1, with eigenvectors along the x‑ and y‑axes.
questions.correctAnswer: Q has no real eigenvalues, and therefore no non‑zero real eigenvectors.
questions.explanation: A 90° rotation changes the direction of every non‑zero real vector, so no real vector remains parallel to itself. Hence the eigenvalues are complex (±i) and there are no real eigenvectors.

questions.questionText: Why is the equation det(A - λI)=0 used to determine the eigenvalues of a matrix A?
options: Because (A - λI) must be invertible for a non‑zero eigenvector to exist.
Because a non‑zero eigenvector exists only when (A - λI) is singular, i.e., its determinant equals zero.
Because the determinant directly gives the sum of the eigenvalues of A.
Because the determinant of (A - λI) equals the trace of A.
questions.correctAnswer: Because a non‑zero eigenvector exists only when (A - λI) is singular, i.e., its determinant equals zero.
questions.explanation: An eigenvector x≠0 satisfies (A‑λI)x=0, which is possible only if (A‑λI) is singular; a matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is zero, leading to the characteristic equation det(A‑λI)=0.

questions.questionText: For the matrix A = [[4, -5],[2, -3]], which of the following vectors is an eigenvector associated with the eigenvalue λ = 2?
questions.explanation: Solving (A-2I)x=0 gives 2x1-5x2=0, so x1=5, x2=2 up to scalar multiples; thus [5,2] is an eigenvector.

questions.questionText: For the 3×3 projection matrix P that projects every vector in ℝ³ onto the xy‑plane, which statement about its eigenvalues is correct?
options: It has eigenvalues 1, 1, 0.
It has eigenvalues 1, 0, -1.
It has eigenvalues 2, 1, 0.
It has eigenvalues i, -i, 0.
questions.explanation: Vectors lying in the xy‑plane are unchanged by P, giving eigenvalue 1 with multiplicity 2; the unit vector along the z‑axis is sent to 0, giving eigenvalue 0.

questions.questionText: For any 2 × 2 matrix A with eigenvalues λ₁ and λ₂, which statement is always true?
options: The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace of A.
The product of the eigenvalues equals the trace of A.
The difference of the eigenvalues equals the determinant of A.
The sum of the squares of the eigenvalues equals the determinant of A.
questions.correctAnswer: The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace of A.
questions.explanation: For an n × n matrix, the characteristic polynomial expands to λⁿ – (trace A)λⁿ⁻¹ + … + (–1)ⁿdet A. Hence for a 2 × 2 matrix λ₁ + λ₂ = trace A and λ₁·λ₂ = det A. Only the first statement holds universally.
questions.subtopic: Eigenvalue properties – trace and determinant relationship

questions.questionText: For a 2×2 matrix A with eigenvalues λ₁=2 and λ₂=−1, which of the following must be the trace of A?
questions.explanation: The trace of a matrix equals the sum of its eigenvalues: 2 + (−1) = 1.

questions.questionText: If an eigenvalue λ of a matrix A is –3, what geometric effect does A have on its corresponding eigenvector?
options: It stretches the eigenvector by a factor of 3 without changing its direction
It shrinks the eigenvector to the zero vector
It stretches the eigenvector by a factor of 3 and reverses its direction
It rotates the eigenvector by 90 degrees
questions.correctAnswer: It stretches the eigenvector by a factor of 3 and reverses its direction
questions.explanation: A negative eigenvalue scales the eigenvector by the absolute value of λ and flips its direction; thus λ = –3 means a stretch by 3 and a reversal.
